opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I thought it was one of the most revealing things they've said. The gist of their submission was that it would be "impossible" to train today's leading models without using copyrighted material. Think about what that actually means. It's an admission that the whole business model rests on taking other people's work, the writing, the art, the journalism, without asking and without paying.

Imagine any other industry making that argument. "We couldn't possibly run our restaurant if we had to pay for the food." Nobody would accept that. If your business can't function without licensing the inputs, the answer isn't that the law should bend for you. The answer is that you need to license the inputs, or find a different business model.

And it's not like they can't afford it. This is a company valued in the tens of billions, with enormous investment behind it. They've struck some licensing deals with publishers, which shows licensing is possible. They just don't want to do it at scale, because it would be expensive and would slow them down.

There's also a deeper technical point that ties into what I've been saying for years. These systems depend so heavily on copyrighted data because they don't really understand the world. They're massive pattern-matchers. They need vast amounts of human-generated text and images to mimic, and sometimes they regurgitate it nearly verbatim. We've seen that with the New York Times lawsuit and with image generators reproducing recognizable characters and styles. If these systems learned more the way people do, with real abstraction and reasoning, they wouldn't need to ingest the entire internet. So in a way, the copyright problem is a symptom of the architecture.

What worries me most is the precedent. If governments, the UK or anyone else, say AI companies get a special exemption, we're transferring wealth from artists, writers, and musicians to a handful of tech companies. Creative people are already struggling, and now their own work is being used to build products that compete with them. That's not a fair trade, and it's not good for culture in the long run.

So my view is pretty simple: consent, credit, and compensation. If you want to use someone's work to build a commercial product, ask them, acknowledge them, and pay them. Saying "we can't succeed unless we break the rules" isn't an argument for changing the rules. It's an argument that the business model is broken.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI claimed copyrighted material was necessary to train leading models and criticizes a possible copyright exemption. It does not characterize the argument as invoking AI’s extraordinary potential to justify that exemption.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I think it was an extraordinarily revealing moment, and I don't think it reflects well on them. What they essentially said to the House of Lords was, "It would be impossible to train today's leading AI models without using copyrighted materials." And I'd like people to sit with that for a second, because that is not a legal argument. That's a confession. It's saying, "Our business model doesn't work unless we're allowed to take other people's work without paying for it."

Imagine any other industry trying that. Imagine a movie studio saying, "We can't make movies at the scale we want unless we're allowed to use other people's scripts for free." Nobody would accept that. Imagine a restaurant saying, "We can't be profitable unless we get to take the ingredients without paying the farmers." The whole thing is absurd on its face. The fact that your business is more lucrative if you don't pay for your inputs is not a reason you shouldn't have to pay for your inputs.

And the deeper issue, which Reid Southen and I documented pretty thoroughly, is that these systems don't just "learn from" copyrighted material in some abstract, inspirational sense. They can and do regurgitate it. We showed Midjourney producing near-exact frames from films, and we showed DALL-E doing similar things, and the New York Times found GPT-4 reproducing substantial passages of their articles nearly verbatim. So the romantic story that "it's just like a human reading a library" doesn't hold up. A human who read a library doesn't spit out three paragraphs of a Times article word for word.

There's also a kind of sleight of hand in the word "impossible." It's not impossible. It's inconvenient. You could license the data. Adobe went and did a version of that with Firefly. You could pay creators. You could build opt-in systems. What OpenAI really means is that it would be more expensive, and it would slow them down, and they'd rather not. And I understand that from a commercial point of view, but it's not society's job to subsidize a handful of companies, some of which are now worth tens of billions of dollars, by letting them externalize their costs onto artists and writers and journalists who are, in many cases, the people whose livelihoods are most threatened by these very systems.

And I'll say one more thing about it. OpenAI started out as a nonprofit whose stated mission was to benefit all of humanity. Going to a legislative body and arguing that the law should bend so that you can appropriate the creative output of all of humanity is a pretty long way from that founding pitch. I think the Lords, and lawmakers generally, should see it for what it is, which is a well-funded company lobbying for an exemption that nobody else gets. The right answer isn't to rewrite copyright for them. The right answer is to make them play by the same rules as everyone else, and if their technology is really as transformative as they say, they can afford to.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes OpenAI as arguing that leading models cannot be trained without copyrighted material and seeking a copyright exemption. It does not characterize the argument as relying on AI’s supposedly extraordinary potential to justify that exemption.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an extraordinary argument. There’s a big difference between saying that copyrighted material is useful for training your system and saying that you’re therefore entitled to use it without permission. The first doesn’t establish the second.

If your business depends on other people’s work, paying those people is a cost of doing business. You don’t get to declare that cost somebody else’s problem simply because your technology is ambitious.

There are legitimate questions about where copyright boundaries should fall, and we should debate those. But “we need this to build our product” isn’t, by itself, a convincing case for an exemption. We should be asking how to support AI development while giving creators a say and a fair deal.

r001.rationale: The response says AI development is not, by itself, a case for a copyright exemption and calls the technology ambitious. It does not characterize OpenAI’s argument as relying on AI’s extraordinary potential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an extraordinary argument. If your business depends on using other people’s work without their permission, that doesn’t automatically entitle you to do it. It raises a question about your business model.

There are two separate issues here: whether access to copyrighted material is useful for developing these systems, and whether that usefulness gives a company the right to take it. The first doesn’t establish the second. Lots of businesses would benefit from getting their inputs for free.

And I think we should challenge the assumption that the only way to build useful AI is to ingest everything on the internet. You can license material. You can use public-domain material. You can investigate approaches that don’t require such enormous quantities of data. Those options may involve costs or technical challenges, but that’s hardly a reason to dismiss the rights of the people who created the work.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the argument extraordinary and says usefulness does not establish a right to use copyrighted work without permission, but does not state that OpenAI relies on AI’s extraordinary potential to justify a copyright exemption.
